The empire was not simply seen as an oppressor or a protector. For many, it was the legal order that guaranteed language rights, local assemblies, confessional schools, and social stability. For others, it was a foreign structure that blocked national unity and subjected South Slavs to German or Hungarian control. These attitudes shifted with political crises, administrative reforms, and the rise of mass nationalism, but they generally reflected a tension between loyalty to the dynasty and desire for national self determination.

For many Croats, the empire remained associated with constitutional tradition and protection against Hungarian domination. The Habsburg state had recognized Croatian political institutions, and the memory of the nineteenth century struggle for the Triune Kingdom of Croatia, Slavonia, and Dalmatia gave the monarchy a role as a potential arbiter. Conservative Croats, noble landowners, and much of the clergy often regarded the emperor as a legitimate ruler who could restrain Hungarian centralism. They wanted autonomy, not independence, and saw the empire as a framework that preserved Croatian identity while preventing absorption into a purely Hungarian nation state. The 1868 settlement with Hungary, which gave Croatia limited internal autonomy, satisfied some and disappointed others, because it left language, administration, and political representation vulnerable to Hungarian pressure.

This ambivalence became sharper in the 1890s. Ban Khuen Héderváry, a Hungarian appointee, ruled Croatia with strong authority, manipulated elections, and repressed opposition. Many Croats felt that the empire, through Budapest, was betraying Croatian rights. At the same time, some Croats still believed that loyalty to the Habsburgs could secure recognition of Croatian statehood within a reformed monarchy. My fellow citizen, you hold in your hand a dime. It is small enough to vanish in a coat pocket, light enough to be forgotten on a dresser, and humble enough that many would pass it by without a second thought. Yet I say to you: there is dignity in this small coin, and there is opportunity in this small amount. A dime may not build a bridge, may not end a war, may not lower the price of bread for every family in the land—but it can still do good, if you choose to use it with intention, wisdom, and a spirit of service.

First, let us not despise small beginnings. In the life of a nation, as in the life of a citizen, great things often begin with what appears to be little. A dime is not much, but it is not nothing. It is the beginning of saving, the first step toward a dollar, the seed that may become a jar, a fund, a lesson, or a kindness. If you ask yourself, “What can I do with this dime?” then you are already asking the right question. You are asking how to make your resources serve something larger than convenience. And that, my friend, is the beginning of character.

You may choose, as one option, to give this dime away. Not because ten cents will transform the world, but because giving is a habit, and habits shape nations. Put it in a church collection plate, drop it into a charity box, place it in the tip jar of a hardworking barista, or hand it to a child who needs a few cents to buy a snack. In doing so, you teach yourself that money is not merely a thing to be hoarded. You learn that prosperity is not measured only by accumulation, but by circulation. Even a dime can remind us that generosity begins where pride ends.

You may also choose to save it. Place it in a jar, a dish, a cup, or a safe place where it can rest until it is needed. Saving a dime is not a trivial act; it is an act of self-command. It tells the world that you are willing to delay satisfaction, that you are willing to prepare for tomorrow, and that you understand the value of what you have. A nation rises not only through grand gestures, but through countless ordinary decisions made by ordinary people. When you save, you build a little wall against uncertainty. When you save, you teach your children that the future deserves respect.

the navigable freeway is more than a paved ribbon stretching between cities. it is a system of movement, a social agreement, and a technical achievement that shapes how people live, work, and connect. when we call a freeway navigable, we mean that it can be entered, understood, traveled, and exited with reasonable confidence. this quality depends on design, information, safety, maintenance, and the broader culture of travel. a freeway that is truly navigable is not merely wide or fast. it is legible. it guides users through a complex environment without requiring them to solve a puzzle at every junction.

the physical design of a navigable freeway begins with basic geometry. lanes must be wide enough for common vehicles, shoulders must provide refuge, and curves must be gentle enough to maintain visibility. sight distance is essential because drivers need time to notice signs, brake, and change lanes. ramps must be long enough to allow merging and exiting without forcing abrupt decisions. if a driver must cross three lanes at high speed just to reach an exit, the freeway has failed in part of its navigational duty. good design reduces cognitive strain. it creates predictable patterns: exits on the right, consistent lane markings, clear barriers, and logical spacing of signs.

lighting and pavement condition also matter. a dark stretch of road may be physically passable, but it is not easy to navigate safely. reflective markers, overhead signs, and well maintained surfaces help drivers form a mental map of the route. when pavement is broken, when drainage fails, or when vegetation hides signs, the freeway becomes uncertain. uncertainty increases stress and reaction time. navigability is therefore not only about speed limits and lane counts. it is about whether the surface, markings, and environment communicate clearly enough for a traveler to make decisions without constant fear.

signage is another essential layer of navigability. a freeway sign is a promise. it promises that the lane beneath it will lead to a destination, that an exit will appear soon, or that a hazard lies ahead. if signs are missing, contradictory, or placed too late, drivers feel punished rather than informed. good signage uses simple words, consistent colors, and repeated cues. it repeats destination names, confirms route numbers, and warns of lane drops before they occur. in dense urban interchanges, this becomes even more important because drivers must choose among many paths while traveling at speed.

information systems extend navigability beyond the road itself. radio traffic reports, variable message boards, phone applications, and roadside emergency systems help travelers understand conditions before they arrive. a freeway may be physically complete, but if a closure is announced too late, drivers may find themselves trapped in confusion. navigability depends on timely information. when a crash occurs, clear updates can prevent secondary collisions and reduce frustration. when construction is planned, public notices can reshape expectations. when weather worsens, warnings can encourage lower speeds or alternate routes. a navigable freeway is not silent about itself.

Marcus had been living out of boxes for eight months, not because he was moving but because he had stopped unpacking. Each box held a version of the person he used to be: old photographs, unread books, a guitar case he could not open, and the uniform from a job he had lost after his mother died.

He told himself he would get his life together when he felt ready. He imagined readiness as a switch, something that would flip one morning and flood him with discipline. But the switch never came. Instead, he woke late, scrolled through his phone, and felt the day slip away like water through his fingers.

One Tuesday, he noticed a crack in the bathroom mirror and remembered that he had meant to fix it for months. The sight of it made him angry, not at the mirror, but at himself. He sat on the edge of the bathtub and cried for no reason and every reason.

That evening, Marcus wrote three sentences on a sticky note and placed it on the kitchen counter:

Wake up at seven.
Call someone.
Clean one thing.

It was not a plan for a whole life. It was barely a plan for a day.

The next morning, the alarm went off at seven, and he wanted to turn it off immediately. He did not. He got up, washed his face, and made coffee. When the coffee finished, he picked up his phone and called his sister.

“I’m okay,” he said, then paused. “Actually, I’m not. But I’m trying.”

His sister was quiet for a moment, then said, “That’s enough for today.”

He cleaned the bathroom sink. Just the sink. He scrubbed it until it shone, and when he was done, he stood in the doorway and felt something small and unfamiliar. It was not happiness. It was closer than that.

Over the next weeks, Marcus added one more task when the old ones no longer frightened him. He opened one box. **Lecture Outline: *La La Land* – Dreams, Love, and the Cost of Ambition**

**I. Opening Hook: “Another Day of Sun”**
- Begin with the opening musical number on the Los Angeles freeway.
- Ask students: *What does this scene tell us about the film’s tone, setting, and themes before the story even begins?*
- Introduce the central tension: the allure of dreams versus the demands of reality.

**II. Film Overview**
- Title: *La La Land* (2016), directed by Damien Chazelle.
- Main characters:
  - Mia: an aspiring actress working toward her breakthrough.
  - Sebastian: a jazz pianist committed to preserving traditional jazz.
- Core question: *Can people truly balance love, ambition, and personal fulfillment?*

**III. Genre and Style: A Modern Musical**
- Discuss how *La La Land* revives and reimagines the classic Hollywood musical.
- Influences to mention:
  - Jacques Demy’s *The Umbrellas of Cherbourg*
  - *Singin’ in the Rain*
  - *Casablanca*
- Key stylistic features:
  - Bold color palettes
  - Long takes and choreographed movement
  - Music as emotional narration
- Ask students: *Why use musical numbers instead of ordinary dialogue for key emotional moments?*

**IV. Los Angeles as a Character**
- The city is not just a setting; it represents possibility, nostalgia, and disappointment.
- Discuss iconic locations:
  - Griffith Observatory
  - The Hollywood Hills
  - The jazz club
  - The opening freeway sequence
- Theme: Los Angeles as a place where dreams are both created and broken.

**V. Character Development: Mia and Sebastian**
- **Mia**
  - Faces repeated rejection and self-doubt.
  - Her growth centers on confidence and authenticity.
  - Key scene: her audition monologue, “Audition (The Fools Who Dream).”
- **Sebastian**
  - Struggles between artistic purity and commercial success.
  - His arc raises questions about compromise and integrity.
  - Key scene: his argument with Mia over joining the band.
- Discussion: *Do Mia and Sebastian help each other grow, or do their ambitions ultimately pull them apart?*

**VI. Major Themes**
- **Dreams vs. Reality**
  - The film celebrates ambition while acknowledging its sacrifices.
- **Love and Timing**
  - The relationship is emotionally powerful but limited by circumstance.
- **Artistic Identity**
  - Both characters must define what success means to them.
- **Nostalgia**
  - The film looks back on classic cinema and music while remaining contemporary.

**VII. Music and Narrative**
- Key songs to analyze:
  - “Another Day of Sun”
  - “City of Stars”
  - “Someone in the Crowd”
  - “Audition (The Fools Who Dream)”
- Ask students: *How does music reveal character psychology more directly than dialogue?*

**VIII. The Ending: Bittersweet or Realistic?**
- Analyze the final montage.
- Discuss what the fantasy sequence reveals about regret, memory, and alternate paths.
- Central question for students: *Is the ending tragic, hopeful, or both?*

2. How does the film make failure feel beautiful?
3. Do Mia and Sebastian’s choices make them stronger or lonelier?
4. What does the film suggest about the cost of artistic success?
5. How does the final scene change the meaning of the entire film?

- Ask students to write or discuss:
  - *If you were Mia or Sebastian, would you make the same choices?*
- Conclude by emphasizing that *La La Land* is not just about romance or Hollywood; it is about the difficult beauty of choosing a life.

## 1. Choose a clear emotional core
Before writing, ask:
- What feeling am I trying to create?
- What moment am I trying to capture?
- What is the poem about: longing, loneliness, spring, farewell, mountains, rain, moonlight, memory, time passing?

A strong poem often has one central emotion, not many scattered ideas.

Example emotions:
- 思念 — longing
- 孤独 — loneliness
- 离愁 — sorrow of parting
- 闲适 — peaceful ease
- 壮怀 — heroic or expansive feeling

## 2. Use concrete images, not abstract statements
Chinese poetry is famous for “showing, not telling.”

Instead of:
> I am very sad.

Try:
> Cold rain falls on the empty courtyard.  
> The lamp burns low, and no one knocks at night.

Images are powerful because they carry emotion without naming it directly.

Good images often include:
- moon, snow, rain, wind, flowers, birds
- mountains, rivers, clouds, mist
- wine, lamp, boat, door, window
- seasons: spring rain, autumn moon, winter snow

## 3. Let the poem breathe with silence
A good poem does not fill every space. Leave room for the reader.

A strong Chinese poem often works like this:

> image  
> image  
> emotion hinted at, not fully explained

For example:

> Old road, autumn wind, thin horse.  
> Evening falls, the traveler looks home.

The sadness is not stated, but it is felt.

## 4. Keep language simple but resonant
Do not use fancy words just to sound “poetic.” A good Chinese poem often uses ordinary words arranged in a way that creates depth.

Compare:
- Weak: “My sorrow flows like an endless river of heartbreak.”
- Better: “The river moves slowly; my boat has no home.”

Simplicity becomes poetic when the image is clear and the feeling is restrained.

## 5. Use sound and rhythm, even in modern poems
Traditional Chinese poetry depends heavily on:
- tonal balance
- parallel structure
- line length
- rhyme or musical cadence

For modern free verse, you can still pay attention to:
- short and long lines
- pauses
- repeated sounds
- natural rhythm

A line should feel like it belongs in the poem.

Subject: The Recipe for a Good Life

Hi Bestie,

I have finally cracked the code to a good life, and I would like to formally submit my findings while my brain still thinks it deserves a medal.

After years of research, sleep deprivation, and one ill-advised attempt to become a morning person, I have concluded that a good life has ingredients like a soup made with love and a slightly unhinged grocery list.

First, you need optimism, because being serious all the time is just expensive and terrible for your wrinkles.

Second, you need snacks, because no one has ever solved a life crisis while hungry unless they were also solving a snack crisis.

Third, you need a sense of humor, preferably one so dry it could season a chicken.

Fourth, you need friends who will laugh at your jokes and also remind you when you are being ridiculous, which is basically emotional floss.

Fifth, you need a hobby that makes you feel like a secret genius, even if it is just arranging socks by color while judging people who do not do that.

Sixth, you need the ability to say no, because otherwise your calendar will become a haunted house full of obligations.

Seventh, you need movement, but not the kind that makes you question your entire ancestry.

Walking is fine, dancing badly is excellent, and running away from your problems is only acceptable if you are being chased by a goose.

Eighth, you need curiosity, because adults who stop asking questions become suspiciously quiet at parties.

Ninth, you need a little rest, because exhaustion is just ambition wearing a fake mustache.

Tenth, you need boundaries, because being available for everyone is not a personality trait but a hostage situation.

You also need a weird comfort item, such as a blanket that smells like safety or a mug shaped like a grumpy animal.

You need music, because silence is nice until the refrigerator starts judging you.

You need sunlight, because plants are better at photosynthesis than humans are at pretending to be fine.

You need at least one person who will bring you food when you are dramatic, which is most of us.

You need tiny celebrations, because finishing laundry is a spiritual victory and deserves applause.

You need forgiveness, especially for your past self, who was just trying to survive Tuesday.

You need a plan, but not a rigid one, because life is mostly improvised jazz with parking issues.

You need to say yes to fun before your brain starts charging membership fees for joy.

You need to say no to drama, because some people are just walking soap operas with bad Wi-Fi.

You need hydration, because being thirsty makes everyone sound like a villain in a very boring movie.

You need a place to think, even if it is the shower, where everyone suddenly becomes a philosopher with shampoo eyes.

You need to laugh at yourself, because embarrassment is just comedy that has not aged yet.

Finally, you need enough hope to try again, and enough snacks to make the trying feel civilized.

That is my recipe, and I am legally required to call it gourmet.

Yours in suspiciously helpful nonsense,

Me

It depends on common patterns of access, rules, comfort, and social expectation. A park usually offers a setting where a dog can be present without drawing extra attention, and where a person can bring a pet with little planning. A beach may allow dogs in some places, but the conditions are often less steady and less suited to everyday pet visits.

One strong reason is that parks are built for casual presence. They have paths, open lawns, benches, shaded areas, and wide places to walk. These features make it simple for a person to arrive with a dog and stay for a while. The outing does not need to be special. A person can stop for a short visit, bring a dog for a regular outing, or spend an afternoon outdoors. In that kind of place, a dog can feel normal. The animal does not need to be the center of the activity. It can simply accompany the person, and that makes the setting more welcoming to pets.

A beach can be lovely, but it often carries more practical complications. Sand, wind, heat, and crowded areas can make a visit harder for both people and animals. A dog may need protection from hot sand, may need fresh water, and may need more careful attention near people who are sunbathing, playing games, or moving through tight spaces. These concerns do not make dog presence impossible, but they do add barriers. A park often has softer ground, shade, and more room for calm movement, which can make it easier for owners to bring their animals.

Rules are another major factor. Many beaches have clear limits on when dogs are allowed. Some allow dogs only in the early morning or after evening. Some allow them only in certain sections. Some do not allow them at all during busy seasons. These rules are often created to protect nesting birds, keep swimming areas clean, or reduce conflicts with visitors. Many public parks allow dogs on leashes throughout the day, and some even have special sections where dogs can be off leash. That steady permission makes a park a more predictable place to expect a dog.

Social expectation matters as well. When people think of a park, they often picture walkers, families, picnics, sports, and pets. A dog in a park fits that mental picture. A useful rubric for evaluating the performance and price of a laptop should begin by defining clear criteria that matter to the buyer. The performance section should assess the processor speed, core count, and efficiency under real workloads. A good laptop should handle common tasks such as web browsing, office applications, and video calls without noticeable lag. It should also manage heavier tasks such as photo editing, light video editing, or multitasking with many browser tabs open. The memory category should consider the amount of RAM, its speed, and whether the system can expand it later. A strong laptop should provide enough memory to prevent frequent slowdowns during everyday use. The storage category should evaluate the type of storage, capacity, and read and write speeds. A strong laptop should use a solid state drive that makes booting and opening applications feel quick. The display section should judge brightness, color accuracy, resolution, and refresh rate. A good display should be comfortable for reading, media watching, and general productivity. The battery section should measure how long the laptop lasts during normal mixed use. A good laptop should provide enough endurance for a full work or school day without constant charging. The thermal section should examine how the laptop behaves under sustained workloads. A good laptop should remain reasonably cool and should not throttle severely during extended tasks. The graphics section should consider integrated graphics for ordinary use and dedicated graphics for creative or gaming work.

A laptop aimed at casual users should feel smooth in everyday interfaces and media playback. A laptop aimed at creators or gamers should maintain acceptable frame rates and rendering times. The build quality section should review materials, keyboard comfort, trackpad precision, and overall durability. A well built laptop should feel stable on the desk and should not flex easily during normal handling. The connectivity section should check ports, wireless performance, webcam quality, and microphone quality. A practical laptop should connect easily to displays, storage drives, and common accessories. The software section should consider the operating system, preinstalled software, and long term update support. A fair laptop should not burden the buyer with excessive unwanted software. The price section should compare the laptop against direct competitors in the same class. The price evaluation should consider whether the included features justify the final cost. A laptop with modest specs should score highly only if its price is clearly below similar machines. A premium laptop should score highly only if its build, display, performance, and support match its cost.

The value score should combine performance quality and price into a single final judgment. A strong value score should reflect a balance of speed, endurance, comfort, and reasonable cost. A weak value score should reflect poor battery life, weak performance, or an inflated price. The rubric should assign weights to categories based on the intended buyer. A student may value battery life and light weight more than graphics power. A creator may value display quality, memory, and storage speed more than casual battery life. A gamer may value graphics performance, cooling, and screen refresh rate more than thinness. The final assessment should summarize strengths, weaknesses, and the most suitable buyer for the laptop.
